models.approach: Trace the trend to the cost of the years in which people would have had children, then follow the effects through the labour market.
plan: Introduction: name the trend and promise causes then effects.
Body 1: the causes, ranked, with housing and childcare first.
Body 2: the effects, joined explicitly to those causes.
Conclusion: whether it is reversible and what would have to change.

paras.text: In most wealthy countries the average mother is now over thirty, and a growing minority will have no children at all. [[It is evident that]] this shift has identifiable causes rather than being a change of taste, and its consequences will be felt for the rest of the century.

[[The main point is]] one of economic timing. The years in which people once started families are now the years of unstable work and unaffordable rent, and a couple cannot commit to a child while moving flat annually. Childcare costs [[exacerbate]] this: in several countries a nursery place consumes a third of one salary, which makes a second child a straightforward financial impossibility. [[Owing to]] both, the decision is postponed until it becomes biological rather than voluntary.

[[As a result]], the population ages from the bottom rather than the top. Fewer workers support more pensioners, so either taxes rise or provision falls, and both outcomes tend to [[engender]] resentment between generations. Rural areas empty first as young people concentrate in cities, leaving schools and clinics that no longer have a population to serve. [[It follows that]] the shortage of workers is met by immigration, which is itself contested precisely where the decline is steepest.

[[In conclusion]], the trend is driven by cost rather than by choice, and it is therefore not [[irreversible]]. Countries that made housing affordable and childcare free, notably in Scandinavia, slowed the fall, which suggests that the birth rate is measuring the price of a stable life rather than any decline in the wish for one.

notes: Causes are ranked rather than listed. Saying which matters most, and why, is what the question is really testing.
The effects paragraph opens with As a result and keeps referring back to the causes, which is where this question type earns its coherence mark.
The conclusion answers a question the prompt did not ask, whether it can be reversed, and that is the difference between finishing and stopping.

models.approach: Argue that the deeper cause is a change in what a life is expected to contain, and follow it through to social effects.
plan: Introduction: money explains part of it, expectation explains more.
Body 1: causes, women's education and the redefinition of adulthood.
Body 2: effects, on families, care and politics.
Conclusion: what a society should do about a change it cannot undo.

paras.text: Explanations for falling birth rates usually stop at the cost of housing, which is true but incomplete: rich countries with cheap housing have the same trend. [[From my perspective]] the deeper causes are cultural, and they are unlikely to reverse.

[[The main point is]] that women's education and employment have altered the shape of an adult life. A woman who spends her twenties qualifying and her early thirties establishing herself has not rejected children; she has [[intentional]] priorities that arrive first. [[At the same time]], parenthood itself has been redefined as an expensive project demanding [[meticulous]] attention, so having three children now implies a standard of provision that once applied to none. [[Consequently]], the decision feels less like a stage of life and more like a career choice competing with the others.

[[As a result]], households grow smaller and kinship networks thinner. A generation with few siblings has few aunts and cousins, so the informal care that families once absorbed becomes a service somebody must pay for, and the [[intangible]] support of a large family disappears from the accounts entirely. Politically, an older electorate votes for pensions over schools, which [[inhibits|Inhibit]] exactly the spending that might have made children affordable.

[[Overall]], the causes lie in a changed idea of adulthood, and no government policy will restore the previous one. [[It stands to reason]] that the sensible response is adaptation rather than reversal: later retirement, serious immigration policy and public care for the elderly, since the family can no longer be assumed to provide it.

notes: Opening by rejecting the obvious explanation gives the essay something to prove, and the counterexample of rich countries with cheap housing earns the right to do so.
The effects paragraph moves from household to state, which gives it a direction rather than a list.
Adaptation rather than reversal is a genuine opinion. Cause and effect questions still allow one in the conclusion.

models.approach: Argue that the common factor behind every explanation is the inability to predict the next ten years.
plan: Introduction: one cause underlies the usual list.
Body 1: causes, insecurity of work, climate and place.
Body 2: effects, on the economy and on who has children.
Conclusion: what would have to change, and what will not.

paras.text: Housing, childcare and careers are all offered as reasons for later parenthood, and each is real. [[I would argue]] that they share one root: having a child is a twenty-year commitment made by people who cannot confidently describe the next two.

[[First and foremost]], work has become [[intermittent]]. Short contracts and gig platforms produce an income that cannot be planned around, and no amount of enthusiasm makes a family [[coherent]] with an unpredictable month. Housing repeats the pattern, since a tenancy renewed annually cannot hold a school place. [[It is worth noting]] that young adults also report a [[fervent]] anxiety about climate and war, and while that is easy to dismiss, surveys consistently find it among the stated reasons for delay.

[[This leads to]] two consequences of very different kinds. Economically, a shrinking cohort of workers must fund a growing cohort of pensioners, and the [[imminent]] arrival of that imbalance is already visible in every long-range budget. Socially, childbearing concentrates among the two groups least exposed to insecurity, the wealthy and the very poor, so the [[dichotomy]] widens between families with resources and families without.

[[Ultimately speaking]], the birth rate is a measure of confidence in the future. Secure tenancies, predictable contracts and affordable care would restore some of it, though [[to some degree]] the anxiety runs deeper than any of those, and a society that wants children must first look like one worth handing to them.

notes: Finding a single cause behind several is the most impressive move available in a causes question, provided you then show how each of the usual reasons follows from it.
The two effects are deliberately different in kind, economic and social, so the paragraph does not simply say the same thing twice.
The final clause is the only rhetorical sentence in the essay. One is enough.
